# Could the player wearing number 7 hold his position if everyone around him vanished?

## Short answer

**No.** He could not hold that position and posture. The instant the players around him
disappeared he would pitch forward and downward and end up on the ground — on his hands,
chest and knees — or, at best, convert the fall into a forward stumble by abandoning the
posture entirely.

The photograph shows a rugby union match: Ireland in green against Italy in blue, with RBS
Six Nations pitch-side boards and a pink stand carrying the Olympic rings behind (Rome's
Stadio Flaminio). The two packs are locked in a fully engaged **scrum** in the middle of the
frame, near the far touchline. A referee in the orange/red shirt stands beside it on the
Italian side, Ireland's number 21 and number 14 wait out in the backfield, an Irish back
stands ready just to the right of the scrum, and an Italian player stands beyond it holding
the ball.

Number 7 is the **Irish flanker bound into that scrum**, on the near side of the pack — the
side facing the camera. The white "7" is clearly readable on the back of his green jersey,
distorted and foreshortened because his torso is almost horizontal. He is the only clearly
numbered 7 in the picture.

Zooming in on him shows:

- His **back is roughly horizontal**, at about hip height off the turf — the flat-backed
  scrummaging position — with his body axis pointing left, into the Italian pack.
- His **head and shoulders are dipped down and forward**, tucked into the mass of bodies ahead
  of him, lower than the line of his back.
- His **knees are bent and his feet are planted behind and under him**, studs in the ground,

  grass**. The zoom shows the bare forearm emerging from the green sleeve with its white trim,
  a taped/strapped wrist, and the fingers spread on the turf. Measuring it, the shoulder-to-
  hand distance is almost exactly one arm's length, confirming a fully extended bracing arm.
- His **inside arm is hidden inside the pack**, which is where a flanker binds it — around the
  hips or back of his own lock or prop.
- His **shoulder and upper body are wedged against other players**, Irish forwards to his right
  and the Italian pack pressing from his left.

So he has three points of contact with the ground (two feet and one hand), but he *also* has
at least two load-bearing contacts with other human beings: the arm he is bound with, and the
shoulder he is driving through.

## Why he would fall

1. **A scrum is a force balance, not a resting position.** He is actively extending his legs
   and driving forward with a force of hundreds of newtons. That is only survivable because
   the opposition pack pushes back with an equal and opposite force, transmitted into him
   through his shoulder and his bind. Delete everyone else and the reaction force vanishes
   while his own leg drive does not. A large unbalanced force accelerates him forward
   immediately.

2. **His centre of mass overhangs his base of support.** His head, shoulders and chest project
   forward of and below the triangle formed by his feet and his one planted hand, and they are

3. **One arm is committed to a bind, not to catching himself.** His inside arm is wrapped
   around a team-mate. The moment that team-mate is gone, the arm is grasping empty air, so he
   has only the single already-loaded hand to arrest a fall.

4. **He is laterally wedged as well.** Being sandwiched between his own forwards and the
   Italian pack is what stops him being pushed sideways or rolling. Without those bodies,
   nothing resists a sideways collapse either.

The failure mode is a **forward and downward sprawl**, in the direction he was driving, within
a fraction of a second. It would not be a vertical crush: the weight he carries is essentially
his own and his legs are underneath him, so he topples rather than gets flattened.

## The fair counter-argument, and why it does not change the verdict

The geometry alone is not what dooms him. A human *can* statically hold a three-point stance
on two feet and one hand — that is essentially a sprinter's "set" position or an American
football lineman's three-point stance, and number 7's ground contacts superficially resemble

pulling his feet forward under his centre of mass, and freeing both arms. Holding the position
and posture exactly as photographed is not possible.

directly observed. The image is also low-resolution and shot from an elevated, oblique angle,
so exact limb angles are approximate. None of this uncertainty changes the conclusion: any
reading of his position has him bound into and leaning against an engaged scrum.

No — number 7 could not hold his position and posture without the players around him. He is a
flanker mid-scrum, driving into and braced against bodies that are pushing back on him and
